READING

**Building the numbers**

*Vantwyn pollination revenue*
400 colonies × £168 = £67,200 per season — confirmed by the problem's own label.

*Borage opportunity cost*
400 × £71 = £28,400 per season. The colonies come out too late for Kirkhallow; that income is simply gone.

*Spray losses*
9 % of 400 = 36 colonies. 36 × £210 = £7,560 per season to replace them. The 9 % figure comes from one operator in one season and could be worse; I treat it as the floor.

*Haulage*
£6,900 per season — stated directly.

*Net operating margin per season under TREVANNOCK*
£67,200 − £28,400 − £7,560 − £6,900 = **£24,340**

*Three-season operational total*
£24,340 × 3 = **£73,020**

---

**The equipment question is the hinge**

If TREVANNOCK is chosen, the Ravensgate offer cannot be accepted — the kit is needed through 2029. After the low-emission zone permit lapses on 2030-01-01, the lorry is worth roughly £20,000 as a farm vehicle; the pallets presumably account for much of the residual, but the figure given for the bundle is ~£20,000 combined.

If ORMSCLEUCH is chosen, Ravensgate pays £96,000 before 28 November 2026.

Equipment delta (TREVANNOCK minus ORMSCLEUCH): £20,000 − £96,000 = **−£76,000**

---

**Nominal three-year balance sheet, TREVANNOCK vs ORMSCLEUCH**

| Item | TREVANNOCK | ORMSCLEUCH | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pollination revenue (3 yrs) | +£201,600 | — | — |
| Borage foregone (3 yrs) | −£85,200 | recovered | — |
| Spray losses (3 yrs) | −£22,680 | zero | — |
| Haulage (3 yrs) | −£20,700 | zero | — |
| **Operational net** | **+£73,020** | **+£85,200** | **−£12,180** |
| Equipment proceeds | £20,000 (c.2030) | £96,000 (now) | −£76,000 |
| **Combined** | **£93,020** | **£181,200** | **−£88,180** |

Wait — I need to be precise about what the ORMSCLEUCH operational line represents. Under ORMSCLEUCH, the 400 swing colonies stay home and earn back the £71 borage that TREVANNOCK loses: £28,400 × 3 = £85,200. They also save the spray and haulage. So ORMSCLEUCH's operational line is correctly £85,200 (recovered borage) + £22,680 (spray saved) + £20,700 (haulage saved) = £128,580; TREVANNOCK's operational excess over that baseline is £73,020. The equipment gap is −£76,000. TREVANNOCK still trails by around £3,000 nominally.

---

**Time value makes the gap larger**

£96,000 received today (late 2026) against £20,000 received circa 2030 is not a £76,000 difference in real terms — it is worse. At even a conservative 5 % discount rate:

- PV of £20,000 in four years: £20,000 ÷ 1.05⁴ ≈ £16,450
- PV of the £24,340 annual operational net (years 1–3): ≈ £66,300
- TREVANNOCK total PV: ≈ £82,750
- ORMSCLEUCH equipment PV: £96,000 today, plus PV of recovered borage ≈ £77,300, total ≈ £173,300

The gap on a present-value basis is well over £90,000 in ORMSCLEUCH's favour — not the nominal £3,000 it appears when everything is added undiscounted.

---

**Risk audit**

*Spray losses:* The 9 % figure is one data point from Whinnerdale Bees. Vantwyn will not vary their spray programme. At 12 % losses the annual spray cost rises to £10,080 (+£2,520); at 15 % it is £12,600 (+£5,040). Every percentage point above 9 % costs £840 per season. The downside is open-ended; the upside (fewer than 9 % deaths) is bounded by zero losses. Risk is asymmetric against TREVANNOCK.

*Single-customer dependency:* All three of the previous pollination contracts that funded the kit have failed to renew. Vantwyn is a three-year deal, not a renewal risk in the short term, but the historical base rate of 0 % renewal is a warning about dependence on this revenue stream.

*Coldharbour and Nyefield:* Two vale growers asking about 2028 is the strongest argument for TREVANNOCK. Being in the vale and performing well with Vantwyn would create a platform. However, (a) the enquiry is uncommitted, (b) we have no idea what colony volumes or spray regimes are involved, (c) any additional contract would require more pallets and haulage capacity that TREVANNOCK preserves but that could alternatively be hired, and (d) the previous three-contract track record makes optimism about vale pollination requiring scrutiny. I give this upside real weight, but not enough to reverse a result that is already £88,000 behind nominally and much more on PV.

*Operational risk:* The lorry is a single asset. Mechanical failure during a move, or a permit complication before 2030, has no fallback.

---

**The queen-rearing shed**

The shed is part of the £187,000 spent in 2024 but is excluded from the Ravensgate offer (which covers only pallets and lorry). Under ORMSCLEUCH it becomes a stranded structure. It may have a separate disposal value or alternative use; the problem does not give a figure, and I treat it as a residual matter that does not change the direction of the recommendation — but it is a cost worth pursuing if ORMSCLEUCH is adopted.

---

**Sunk costs**

The £187,000 is gone under either course. Mentioning it only to set it aside: it is irrelevant to the forward choice.

---

**Summary judgement**

On nominal figures the three Vantwyn seasons generate £73,020 net after borage, spray, and haulage — just short of the £76,000 equipment penalty from holding rather than selling the kit. On a time-value basis the gap widens to roughly £13,000 against TREVANNOCK before any risk premium for spray uncertainty or the asymmetric downside from colony losses. The strategic upside from Coldharbour and Nyefield is real but speculative, and the pollination side has a track record of 0 % contract renewal. ORMSCLEUCH puts £96,000 in the bank, eliminates all spray and haulage risk, recovers the borage income, and removes the management burden of a second business that has been idle for a full season. The numbers are closer than they look, but every qualitative factor points the same way as the financial arithmetic.

---

READING
  Revenue per Vantwyn season: 400 × £168 = £67,200. Deduct borage lost (400 × £71 = £28,400), spray replacements (36 colonies × £210 = £7,560), and haulage (£6,900): seasonal net = £24,340, three-season total = £73,020. Equipment delta: Ravensgate pays £96,000 now; kit is worth ~£20,000 after the permit lapses in 2030, a nominal gap of £76,000 and a present-value gap of roughly £80,000 at any modest discount rate. TREVANNOCK's operational premium of £73,020 does not cover the equipment penalty even before discounting, and every risk factor (open-ended spray losses, single-customer dependence, zero historical renewal rate on pollination contracts) cuts against it. Coldharbour and Nyefield are genuinely attractive as a future platform but are uncommitted enquiries against a confirmed £96,000 sale that closes 28 November 2026. ORMSCLEUCH recovers the borage, eliminates haulage and spray exposure, and simplifies the business.

CALL
  ORMSCLEUCH

GROUNDS
  The three Vantwyn seasons produce a net operational gain of £73,020 after borage, spray, and haulage, but that sum falls short of the £76,000 nominal penalty — and well short of the present-value penalty — from forgoing the £96,000 Ravensgate sale in favour of a kit worth only £20,000 once the low-emission zone permit expires, and every qualitative risk compounds that shortfall rather than offsetting it.
